title: How to Be Content When You Long to Be Married
excerpt: Contentment is not pretending you do not want the thing. It is the harder, truer work of being whole while you wait, with the longing still alive.
body:
There is a cruel piece of advice floating around the church that goes: stop wanting marriage and God will give it to you. As if desire were the obstacle, as if contentment meant successfully lying to yourself about what you want. I do not believe it, and I do not think the Bible teaches it. Paul says he learned to be content in any situation (Philippians 4:11-12), and the word he uses does not mean he stopped wanting things. It means he found a stability underneath his wanting, a floor that held whether the want was satisfied or not. That is what we are after. Not the death of the longing. A floor beneath it.

## Contentment is learned, not summoned

Notice that Paul says he learned contentment. It was not a temperament he was born with or a switch he flipped. It was a skill built over years, through plenty and hunger, abundance and need. This should relieve you, because it means your present discontent is not a verdict on your faith. It means you are in the middle of the learning, not failing the test.

So stop expecting to feel content as if it should arrive whole. Treat it as a practice, something you build by repetition, the way you build a muscle. The repetition is what the rest of this is about.

## Refuse the lie that marriage completes you

Under a lot of the ache is a false belief, half-cultural and half-romantic, that a spouse would fix what feels broken or empty in you. Marriage does not do that. I have done plenty of weddings and plenty of counseling, and I can tell you the lonely single person who believes marriage will cure their loneliness becomes the lonely married person who is shocked it did not.

Marriage does not complete you. It exposes you. It takes the cracks you already have and presses on them. The person who is whole in Christ before marriage brings wholeness into it; the person who is desperate for marriage to fix them brings the desperation in, and it gets worse, not better, with an audience. Your completeness has to be sourced somewhere marriage cannot touch (Colossians 2:10), or marriage will disappoint you exactly as much as singleness does.

## Let the longing drive you to God, not away from people

There are two ways the longing for marriage can go. It can curdle into bitterness, self-pity, and withdrawal, where every wedding is a wound and every couple a reproach, and you slowly pull back from the very community that could hold you. Or it can become a kind of prayer, an honest ache you keep bringing to God, that drives you deeper into him and further into people rather than out of them.

The difference is whether you let the longing isolate you. Hannah longed for a child so deeply she could not eat, and she took the longing into the presence of God and poured it out (1 Samuel 1:15). She did not pretend she was fine, and she did not let it pull her into a hole. She wept it out before the Lord and then went back to her life. Do that. Bring it to God raw, then go love the people in front of you.

## Build the full life now

Contentment grows in a full life, not an empty one waiting to be filled. So fill it. Deep friendships, meaningful work, real service, a household of people who count on you, a faith you are actually building rather than pausing. A person whose life is rich in these things can hold the longing for marriage without being ruled by it. A person whose life is thin and reserved, waiting for a spouse to give it meaning, will be ruled by the longing because there is nothing else in the room.

This is not a consolation prize. It is the life God has actually given you, and it is enough to be lived fully, longing and all.

## This week

Name the longing honestly to God, out loud, the way Hannah did, without cleaning it up. Then do one thing that builds the fullness of the life you already have, and would build it whether or not you ever marry. Invest in a friendship, take a role, serve someone.

Contentment is not the absence of wanting. It is a floor beneath the wanting that does not move. You can want marriage with your whole heart and still stand on that floor. That is not pretending. That is being whole while you wait.
